caption:
How did the Inca fit the stones of Sacsayhuamán together so tightly?

Sacsayhuamán is a citadel on the northern edge of Cusco, at 3,701 m. Its three great terrace walls are dry stone — no mortar. A single sheet of paper will not fit between many of the blocks. Pedro Pizarro wrote that "the point of a pin could not have been inserted in one of the joints."

Estimates for the largest limestone block run from 128 tonnes to almost 200. The stone was moved an estimated 35 km from Rumicolca. The longest wall is about 400 m and around 6 m tall; the stonework totals over 6,000 cubic metres.

Pedro Cieza de León, writing in 1553, recorded that the provinces supplied 20,000 men: 4,000 quarrying, 6,000 hauling stone with great cables of leather and cabuya. He also wrote that the living rock was excavated for the foundation.

After the siege of Cusco the Spanish used the site as a quarry, taking it apart block by block for colonial buildings. Garcilaso de la Vega, 1609: "there is indeed not a house in the city that has not been made of this stone." What remains is largely what was too heavy to move.

Still open: how the joints were achieved. The architect Vince Lee proposed the blocks were carved first, towed up ramps and lowered into prepared pockets on stacks of logs, removed one at a time. Experiments reached only limited success, and never at the scale of the largest stones. Surface pottery puts the earliest occupation of the hill at about 900 CE. Ruins found at the periphery in 2008 appear ceremonial, but their exact function remains unknown.

Images: photographs by Bgabel (2005) and Esoltas (2009); an unattributed print of the fortress, c. 1940; an 1854 lithograph after William Lewis Herndon; and two 1900 views by Fernando Garreaud. All public domain.

cards.headline: The walls <y>lean inward</y>, and the earthquakes left them standing
cards.note: Rounded corners, interlocking shapes and the inward lean are thought to have helped the ruins survive Cuzco's earthquakes.
cards.alt: Tiered dry stone Inca walls of tightly fitted blocks under a bright sky.
